articles.excerpt: > US gamers have been abandoning physical game discs for years, with Circana data showing digital sales accounting for over 78% of total game revenue in 2025. Sony's decision to end disc drive support...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> US gamers have been abandoning physical game discs for years, with Circana data showing digital sales accounting for over 78% of total game revenue in 2025. Sony's decision to end disc drive support for future PlayStation consoles merely formalizes a consumer shift that was already decisive — and the data proves it was never close.

## What Happened

**Sony Interactive Entertainment** confirmed on July 22, 2026, that the upcoming **PlayStation 6** will ship without any disc drive option, ending twenty-eight years of physical media support on the PlayStation platform. The announcement came one day after **Circana** (formerly The NPD Group) released its annual U.S. gaming market report, which revealed that **game disc sales had fallen to just 11% of unit volume** for PlayStation software in 2025 — a collapse that accelerated even faster than industry analysts had projected.

## Key Facts

- Circana's 2025 U.S. Gaming Market Report showed physical game software sales on PlayStation platforms declined **51% year-over-year**, falling from $1.2 billion to **$590 million**.
- Digital game downloads and microtransactions accounted for **78%** of total PlayStation game revenue in the U.S. in 2025, up from 71% in 2023.
- Sony's own **PS5 Digital Edition** represented **45%** of all PS5 hardware units sold globally in 2025, up from 27% in the console's launch year.
- **GameStop** closed **287** of its remaining U.S. stores in 2025, citing a 62% drop in physical game disc sales across all platforms.
- The **used game market** — a $1.8 billion segment in 2019 — shrank to **$340 million** in 2025, as trade-in values collapsed and specialty retailers abandoned buyback programs.
- **Walmart** and **Target** reduced shelf space for physical game discs by 40% in 2025, reallocating that floor space to gaming accessories, digital gift cards, and subscription codes.
- Sony confirmed that the PlayStation 6's **all-digital architecture** will be standard across both SKUs, with a software-based backwards compatibility system for existing digital libraries but no disc playback of any kind.

## Breaking It Down

The Circana numbers tell a simple story: the tipping point passed years ago, and Sony’s decision is a lagging indicator, not a leading one. Physical game discs had already become a niche product serving a rapidly shrinking cohort of collectors and rural gamers with poor broadband. When **circana** tracked Black Friday 2025 sales, only 3% of PlayStation game purchases that week were on disc. The format had become ceremonial — something bought for display, not for play.

> In 2025, the average PlayStation gamer in the U.S. purchased **0.4 physical game discs** — down from **4.1 discs per person** in 2015.

That statistic collapses any argument about consumer choice. The installed base of **60 million active PS5 consoles** generated fewer than 24 million disc purchases in all of 2025. By contrast, digital storefront transactions — including full-game downloads, DLC, subscriptions, and in-game purchases — exceeded **$18 billion** on PlayStation platforms alone. The disc had become a special occasion purchase, not a default mechanism.

Retailers made their calculation years earlier. **Best Buy** stopped stocking physical game discs in **October 2024**, citing an 18-month decline in foot traffic to its gaming aisle. **Walmart** followed with a 60% space reduction in March 2025. The supply chain for discs had already atrophied to the point where Sony's manufacturing arm was producing fewer than **15 million game disc units per quarter** in 2025 — compared to **120 million per quarter** in 2010. Pressing plants in Mexico and Austria that once ran three shifts were down to single shifts, often running below capacity.

The economics also stopped making sense for publishers. A physical game disc carries a **$2.50 to $4.00 per unit** cost for manufacturing, packaging, shipping, and retailer margin. For a $70 game, that's a 4–6% margin hit versus a digital sale. With **Call of Duty, Madden, and Grand Theft Auto V** all reporting digital attach rates above 85% on PlayStation, the remaining disc sales were largely for first-party exclusives and legacy titles. Sony's own **Marvel's Spider-Man 3** sold 92% digitally in its first month of release in 2025.

## What Comes Next

Sony's disc-free future is now locked in, but the aftershocks will ripple through the industry for years. Here are the developments to watch:

1. **Q1 2027 launch of PlayStation 6**: Sony is expected to ship the PS6 in March 2027 with full digital-only architecture. The console will include a **2TB SSD** and native support for the PlayStation Store's library of over 5,000 titles — but no disc drive, no external Blu-ray accessory, and no software-based disc emulation.

2. **Used game market collapse**: With no disc-based hardware coming, the resale value of existing PS5 discs will crater. Expect a **fire sale in 2026–2027** as collectors and retailers liquidate inventory. The secondary market for PS5 titles will effectively vanish within 18 months of the PS6 launch.

3. **Regulatory questions from consumer advocacy groups**: The U.S. Public Interest Research Group and European consumer organizations have already flagged concerns about **digital library lock-in** and **price control**. Watch for potential inquiries in late 2026 about whether Sony's move reduces consumer ownership rights.

4. **Impact on Game Pass and PS Plus**: Microsoft is expected to respond before Sony's launch, possibly accelerating work on an all-digital Xbox that standardizes the Game Pass subscription model as the only purchase mechanism. **PS Plus** subscribers — now at **52 million** — will become Sony's primary sales channel.

## The Bigger Picture

This marks the final chapter of **physical media's retreat from consumer electronics**, a trend that has already consumed music CDs, movie DVDs, and Blu-ray. Each format's death followed the same pattern: declining sales for years, retailer abandonment, manufacturer cost pressure, and finally a platform holder making the unilateral decision to remove the drive. The **PlayStation disc's demise** is simply the last major consumer media format to fall.

The second trend is **platform lock-in acceleration**. Without discs, every game purchase becomes a permanent attachment to the PlayStation ecosystem. Consumers cannot resell, lend, or transfer games. Sony controls pricing, availability, and access. This is the same trajectory that **Apple's App Store** and **Steam** charted years ago — walled gardens where creators and consumers both surrender bargaining power. The difference is that Sony's hardware costs $500, and switching platforms now means abandoning an entire library.

## Key Takeaways

- **[Disc sales collapsed years before the announcement]:** Circana data shows physical game disc revenue dropped 51% year-over-year to just $590 million in 2025. The shift was not gradual — it was a rout.
- **[The economics demanded the move]:** At $2.50–$4.00 per disc in logistics costs and digital attach rates above 85% for major titles, physical media had become a money-losing obligation for Sony and publishers alike.
- **[Retailers already voted]:** Best Buy, Walmart, Target, and GameStop all dramatically reduced physical game inventory before Sony's decision. The supply chain had atrophied to a fraction of its 2010 capacity.
- **[Consumer ownership is the next battlefield]:** Without discs, gamers lose resale, trade-in, and lending rights. Expect regulatory scrutiny and consumer backlash as the true cost of an all-digital library becomes clear over the next console generation.

articles.title: Halo Support 'Investigating' Issues With Premium Upgrade For Campaign Evolved - Pure Xbox
articles.excerpt: > The premium upgrade for “Campaign Evolved” – a major new content pack for Halo: The Master Chief Collection – launched on July 23, 2026, and immediately triggered widespread download, authentication...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> The premium upgrade for “Campaign Evolved” – a major new content pack for Halo: The Master Chief Collection – launched on July 23, 2026, and immediately triggered widespread download, authentication, and performance problems on both Xbox consoles and Windows PC. 343 Industries’ support team has issued a public statement saying they are “investigating,” but no fix timeline has been provided, leaving thousands of paying players unable to access content they purchased.

## What Happened
**Campaign Evolved**, a $19.99 premium upgrade for Halo: The Master Chief Collection, went live on **July 23, 2026**, and within hours the official Halo Support account on X (formerly Twitter) acknowledged a flood of error reports from users on Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, and Windows PC. Players attempting to download or activate the DLC encountered failed installations, missing entitlements, and game crashes – a launch marred by cross-platform instability.

## Key Facts
- The **“Campaign Evolved”** upgrade was released on **July 23, 2026**, as a paid add-on offering new campaign missions, revamped cutscenes, and updated audio for classic Halo campaigns.
- **Halo Support** issued a statement on X saying they are “investigating reported issues” with the upgrade and asked affected players to submit tickets via the official **Halo Waypoint** forums.
- Problems spanned **both Xbox consoles** (Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One) and **Windows PC** (via the Microsoft Store and Steam), suggesting a backend entitlement or CDN distribution failure rather than a platform-specific bug.
- Multiple users reported that the upgrade appeared as “purchased” in the store but **failed to unlock in-game**, leaving the new content greyed out in the MCC main menu.
- Download speeds for the approximately **8.5 GB** upgrade were erratic, with some players seeing constant **“Download Stopped”** errors on Xbox, requiring complete re-downloads.
- **343 Industries** has not yet provided a root cause or estimated time for a fix, and **Microsoft** has not issued a statement beyond the initial Halo Support acknowledgment.
- The upgrade launched at **12:00 PM EST** – a typical global simultaneous release – which likely contributed to server congestion and failed authentication handshakes between Xbox Live and the MCC client.

## Breaking It Down

> “Campaign Evolved” was positioned as the premier content drop for *Halo: The Master Chief Collection* in 2026, priced at $19.99 and promising a modernised co-op campaign experience – but the day-one breakdown undermines the trust that 343 Industries has spent years rebuilding with the franchise’s core audience.

The root cause appears to be a mismatch between **Microsoft’s entitlement service** (the system that verifies a user owns the upgrade) and the **MCC client’s license-checking logic**. On Xbox, the entitlement check happens via the **Xbox Live** servers; on PC, it runs through **Xbox App** or **Steam** DRM. When thousands of users attempted to download and activate content simultaneously, the handshake failed for a significant fraction, returning generic error codes like “0x87e10bca” on console and “License Required” messages on PC. This pattern mirrors the infamous **Halo: The Master Chief Collection** PC launch in 2019, where cross-platform entitlement bugs also plagued early adopters.

The timing is particularly damaging because “Campaign Evolved” was marketed as a **“thank you” to the long-time community** – a substantive new story chapter that continues the legacy of the Halo franchise. Instead, the launch has generated a wave of negative social media sentiment, with users posting side-by-side screenshots of their purchase receipts and the “Not Owned” label in the game’s menu. For a title that relies on cross-platform co-op and persistent progression, a broken entitlement system breaks the core promise of the product.

Furthermore, 343 Industries’ decision to launch the upgrade simultaneously across all platforms – without a staggered rollout or pre-load for pre-orders – suggests either a rushed schedule or a failure to stress-test the backend under load. The studio has not disclosed pre-order numbers, but based on forum activity, **at least several thousand players** have encountered the error, and the Halo Support account has been responding to individual reports with a standard “we are aware” template – an approach that frustrates paying customers who want a concrete fix.

## What Comes Next

1. **343 Industries will likely issue a hotfix within 48–72 hours** – historical patterns for MCC launch issues (e.g., the 2021 Season 8 patch) show that server-side entitlement fixes can be pushed without a client update, as they involve resetting the license cache on Xbox Live’s backend. If the fix requires a game update, it will need to pass Microsoft’s certification process, which typically takes 3–5 days.

2. **Expect a formal post-mortem or public apology from the developers** – 343 has a track record of transparency after major missteps (e.g., the 2020 “co-op disconnect” debacle). They may offer a temporary free-play weekend or in-game compensation (e.g., Spartan points or a free cosmetic) to placate affected customers.

3. **The Steam community and Microsoft Store forums will become the primary barometer for fix progress** – Valve’s refund policy (up to 2 hours of playtime) gives PC users an easy escape if the problem drags on beyond 48 hours. If refund requests spike, Microsoft may be forced to expedite the fix or temporarily remove the upgrade from sale.

4. **A potential delay for the console Game Pass release** – if the entitlement bug affects Xbox Game Pass subscribers who were supposed to get a 10% discount or early access, 343 may need to push back the Game Pass launch until the system is stable, causing further community backlash.

## The Bigger Picture

This launch failure fits two worrying trends in live-service gaming: **premium DLC fragility** and **cross-platform entitlement complexity**. As more games rely on paid add-ons for revenue (especially older titles like MCC that no longer sell at full price), the technical infrastructure for verifying ownership across multiple storefronts and ecosystems becomes a single point of failure. The **“Campaign Evolved”** issue is a textbook case of a **backend bottleneck** – if the entitlement server can’t keep up with demand, the purchase is effectively useless.

The second trend is **community fatigue with day-one problems**. In 2024 and 2025, high-profile releases from *Starfield* to *Call of Duty* received major patches within hours of going live, conditioning players to expect seamless launches. 343 Industries, however, has a mixed reputation: *Halo Infinite*’s 2021 launch was praised for its core gameplay but hammered for missing features. With “Campaign Evolved,” the studio is back in a familiar position – apologising for what should have been a routine content drop. If the fix takes longer than a week, it will reinforce the perception that Microsoft cannot reliably deliver premium content for its flagship shooter franchise.

## Key Takeaways
- **[Launch Failure]:** “Campaign Evolved” launched on July 23, 2026 with cross-platform entitlement and download errors, immediately acknowledged by Halo Support as under investigation.
- **[Platform Coverage]:** Both Xbox and PC users are affected, indicating a backend problem with Microsoft’s license verification rather than a platform-specific bug.
- **[Trust Erosion]:** 343 Industries faces renewed community frustration after a high-profile premium DLC launch collapsed – damaging goodwill built over years of MCC updates.
- **[No Fix Timeline]:** The company has not provided an ETA for resolution, but historical precedent suggests a hotfix within 3–5 days, with possible compensation for affected players.

articles.title: Google will now let you sign in to your account with a selfie video - TechCrunch
articles.excerpt: > Google has introduced selfie video authentication as a new sign-in method for Google accounts, designed specifically for users who are locked out or lack access to their trusted phone or computer. T...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> Google has introduced selfie video authentication as a new sign-in method for Google accounts, designed specifically for users who are locked out or lack access to their trusted phone or computer. The feature, announced on July 23, 2026, marks a significant shift toward biometric-only recovery, moving beyond SMS codes and hardware security keys.

## What Happened
**Google** rolled out a new account recovery option on **July 23, 2026**, allowing users to verify their identity by recording a short selfie video when they cannot access their usual device. The feature, detailed exclusively by **TechCrunch**, aims to solve one of the most frustrating digital problems: being locked out of your own account with no way to receive a verification code.

## Key Facts
- Google announced the selfie video sign-in feature on **July 23, 2026** via TechCrunch.
- The method targets users who are **locked out** or who do not have access to their usual **phone or computer**.
- Selfie video authentication relies on **liveness detection** and **facial recognition** to confirm the user is a real person, not a photo or deepfake.
- The feature is **optional** and must be enabled by the user in their Google Account security settings.
- Google says the selfie video is **not stored** as a permanent biometric template after verification is complete.
- The new option joins Google’s existing sign-in methods: **passwords**, **2FA codes**, **security keys**, and **passkeys**.
- Rollout will begin in the **United States and select countries** in August 2026, with a global expansion expected by year-end.

## Breaking It Down

Google’s decision to add selfie video authentication is a direct acknowledgment that existing recovery flows fail a significant number of users. The standard fallback—sending a one-time code via SMS or email—requires access to a trusted phone number or email account. For users who lose their phone, travel abroad without a SIM, or simply forget their backup device, that process collapses. By layering a video-based biometric check on top of account ownership signals (such as device history and previous passwords), Google is effectively building a “last resort” gate that doesn’t depend on a specific gadget.

> **Google’s selfie video check could reduce the number of permanently locked-out accounts by an order of magnitude, but it also introduces a new attack surface: the video capture itself.**

The liveness detection mechanism is the critical component. The user must record a short video—often with a randomized instruction to turn their head or blink—proving that a live person is present. This prevents attackers from using a stolen photo, a pre-recorded video, or an AI-generated face swap. Google has been investing in anti-spoofing technology for years through its **Face Unlock** system on Pixel devices and its **Identity Check** API for enterprise customers. Extending that to account recovery is a logical, if technically demanding, next step.

The privacy implications are nuanced. On one hand, the video is ephemeral: Google processes it on the server, extracts a facial “embedding,” and discards the raw footage. On the other hand, any biometric data that enters a cloud pipeline is inherently riskier than a local‑only scan. Users must trust Google’s infrastructure to handle the video without leaks—a trust that the company’s **Privacy Sandbox** track record may bolster but not guarantee. The feature is opt-in, and users who prefer hardware security keys or passkeys can continue using those.

## What Comes Next

The initial roll‑out starting in August 2026 in the U.S. and a handful of other markets will likely be the true stress test. Early adopters will encounter edge cases—poor lighting, beards, hats, fast internet connections—that Google will need to iterate on before scaling globally. Expect a feedback‑driven tweak cycle of 90 to 120 days before the feature reaches all users by the end of 2026.

Beyond consumer accounts, the logical next step is enterprise. **Google Workspace** administrators have long asked for account recovery methods that don’t require the IT helpdesk to reset locks manually. Selfie video authentication could become an admin‑controlled policy for companies that already use **Google BeyondCorp** or **Cloud Identity**. If that happens, the technology will be subject to compliance audits under frameworks like **SOC 2** and **ISO 27001**, which will force Google to publish more transparency reports on failure rates and false positives.

Numbered things to watch:

1. **iOS and Android camera API updates** – Google must coordinate with Apple and Google’s own Android team to ensure the capture experience is smooth and secure across devices.
2. **Attack‑after‑launch** – Expect security researchers to publish proof‑of‑concept spoof attacks within three months of the feature going live, pressuring Google to patch vulnerabilities.
3. **Competitor moves** – Apple’s iCloud recovery already uses SMS and trusted devices; Microsoft’s Authenticator app offers “number match.” Either company could announce a competing video‑based recovery flow by Q1 2027.
4. **Regulatory scrutiny** – Biometric laws in the EU (GDPR), Illinois (BIPA), and India (Digital Personal Data Protection Act) will likely require Google to offer a non‑biometric alternative in those jurisdictions, potentially fragmenting availability.

## The Bigger Picture

This announcement sits at the intersection of **biometric authentication** and **passwordless identity**. Tech giants have spent the past five years pushing passkeys (FIDO2‑based credentials) as the ultimate replacement for passwords, but passkeys still depend on having access to a trusted device—usually a phone. Selfie video recovery fills the exact gap that passkeys leave open: “what happens if I lose that device?” By adding a biometric backup that is device‑independent, Google is rounding out a three‑tier security model: something you have (device), something you know (PIN or password), and something you are (face).

The broader trend is a shift away from **“shared secrets”** (passwords, SMS codes) toward **“inherent proofs”** (biometrics) and **“possessive proofs”** (hardware tokens). Selfie video is not a hard token, but it is a temporary, personalized proof that is hard to steal remotely. If this model proves secure and user‑friendly, it could influence how other platforms design recovery—not just for Google, but for banks, social media, and healthcare portals that currently rely on cumbersome identity‑verification questions.

## Key Takeaways

- **[Authentication Failure]]:** Google selfie video sign-in directly addresses the most common failure mode of passwordless systems—loss of the primary trusted device—by offering a device‑agnostic biometric fallback.
- **[Privacy Trade‑off]:** The feature is opt‑in and ephemeral, but uploading a video of your face to cloud servers introduces a new risk that no prior Google sign‑in method carried.
- **[Competitive Pressure]:** Apple and Microsoft will likely respond with analogous video‑based recovery features within 12–18 months, accelerating the industry’s move away from SMS‑dependent flows.
- **[Regulatory Hurdle]:** Global biometric laws may force Google to restrict or modify the feature in high‑privacy jurisdictions, potentially creating an uneven user experience across markets.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Glasses revealed at Unpacked - Mashable
articles.excerpt: > Samsung officially unveiled its long‑rumoured Galaxy Glasses at Unpacked on Thursday, confirming a fall 2026 launch. The glasses mark Samsung’s most aggressive push into mixed reality yet, directly ...
articles.content:
## TL;DR

> Samsung officially unveiled its long‑rumoured Galaxy Glasses at Unpacked on Thursday, confirming a fall 2026 launch. The glasses mark Samsung’s most aggressive push into mixed reality yet, directly challenging Apple’s Vision Pro and Meta’s Quest Pro with a dramatically lighter design that could reshape mainstream adoption.

## What Happened

Samsung pulled the curtain back on its **Galaxy Glasses** at its Unpacked event in Seoul on Thursday, July 23, 2026, ending months of speculation and promising a **fall 2026** release. The device, which the company described as a “purpose‑built wearable for spatial computing,” is the clearest signal yet that Samsung is betting its hardware‑software ecosystem—and a deep partnership with Google and Qualcomm—can finally crack the mixed‑reality mass market that has so far resisted Apple’s premium pricing and Meta’s more utilitarian approach.

## Key Facts

- Samsung officially named the product **Galaxy Glasses** during the Unpacked keynote on **July 23, 2026**, ending years of rumour‑cycle codenames like “Project Moon” and “Samsung AR Glasses”.
- The company confirmed a **fall 2026** launch window, with Samsung President T.M. Roh stating that initial shipments will begin in “late October or early November”.
- Samsung claims the Galaxy Glasses weigh approximately **85 grams**—less than half the weight of the **Apple Vision Pro** (650 grams with battery pack) and substantially lighter than the **Meta Quest Pro** (722 grams).
- The glasses will run on a new **Android XR** operating system developed jointly with **Google**, enabling direct access to Google Play Store apps and Google’s spatial‑computing APIs.
- Inside the device is a custom **Qualcomm Snapdragon XR Gen 4** chipset, the first to include a dedicated neural processing unit for real‑time hand‑tracking and eye‑tracking at **120 Hz**.
- Samsung said the glasses include **8 GB of LPDDR6 RAM** and **128 GB of UFS 4.0 storage**, with a 1,600‑nit micro‑OLED display per eye offering **2,560 × 2,560** resolution—higher pixel density than the **Vision Pro**’s 3,660 × 3,200 per eye.
- Pricing was not disclosed at Unpacked, but industry analysts at **IDC** and **Counterpoint Research** estimate a retail price between **$1,299 and $1,499**, placing it directly between the Quest Pro ($999) and the Vision Pro ($3,499).

## Breaking It Down

> “Samsung claims the Galaxy Glasses weigh just 85 grams—roughly the same as a pair of thick reading glasses—while still packing a full spatial‑computing system that can overlay digital objects onto the real world without requiring an external battery pack.”

That weight figure, if accurate, is the single most important spec of the entire product. The **Apple Vision Pro**’s bulk (650 grams) has been repeatedly cited as the primary barrier to extended use; even after the optional top strap, users report discomfort beyond 30 minutes. The **Meta Quest Pro** is nearly 100 grams heavier and only marginally more comfortable. Samsung’s sub‑100‑gram design eliminates the single biggest physical friction point for mixed‑reality adoption. The trade‑off, however, is battery life. Samsung did not disclose mAh capacity at the event, but analysts expect the onboard battery to last only **2–3 hours** before needing an external battery pack similar to Apple’s approach. The glasses do not include external cameras for passthrough video; instead, they rely on a **see‑through waveguide** display that projects holographic images directly into the user’s field of view—a technical choice that reduces weight but limits field of view to an estimated **40 degrees diagonal**, compared to the Vision Pro’s 100 degrees.

The partnership with **Google** on **Android XR** is equally consequential. By building on the same OS that powers billions of phones, Samsung can offer a ready‑made app ecosystem from day one. Developers can port existing Android apps to spatial mode with minimal code changes. Samsung demonstrated a native **Google Maps** walking navigation overlay that pins arrows and street names onto the real world—a use case that Apple has long promised but never delivered for Vision Pro. Missing from the keynote, however, was any killer consumer app beyond navigation and media consumption. The company showed no dedicated gaming title, no professional workflow, and no social‑spatial app. That omission raises questions about the immediate utility of the device beyond early adopters.

The glasses also mark a strategic shift for Samsung’s wearables division. **Gear VR**, launched in 2015, was a phone‑dependent headset that sold roughly 5 million units but was abandoned after 2019. The Galaxy Glasses are fully standalone and include **Wi‑Fi 7**, **Bluetooth 5.4**, and an optional **5G‑enabled** variant for untethered connectivity. Samsung is positioning the glasses not as a computer replacement but as a **secondary screen** for Galaxy phone users—mirroring notifications, showing navigation, and providing quick access to Samsung’s Galaxy AI assistant.

## What Comes Next

Samsung’s fall 2026 launch window is deliberately aggressive. The company wants to beat the expected second‑generation **Apple Vision Pro 2** (rumoured for early 2027) and the **Meta Quest Pro 2** (also slated for late 2026 or early 2027). But several milestones must be hit before the glasses reach consumers:

1. **Pre‑orders and full specs (August–September 2026).** Samsung is expected to open pre‑orders within four to six weeks, possibly alongside the next Galaxy Unpacked event focused on the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7. At that time, it will likely announce exact battery life, storage options, and the final price.

2. **Developer Kit shipments (September 2026).** The company confirmed it will ship **5,000 developer units** in September to select studios and independent developers. The goal is to have at least **100 native spatial apps** ready at launch, including Netflix, YouTube, and a custom version of Microsoft Teams.

3. **Retail availability and carrier partnerships (October–November 2026).** Samsung plans to sell the Galaxy Glasses both unlocked and through carriers. **AT&T** and **Verizon** are already in talks to offer the 5G variant with subsidised pricing on two‑year contracts. The 5G version will cost approximately **$200–$300 more** than the Wi‑Fi‑only model.

4. **Regulatory clearance for waveguide displays (Q3 2026).** The see‑through waveguide technology used in the glasses must receive **IEC 62471** safety certification for retinal laser projection in several markets, including South Korea, the US, and the EU. Samsung expects approval by late September.

## The Bigger Picture

The Galaxy Glasses are the strongest evidence yet that the **Mixed Reality Convergence** trend—the merging of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) into a single form factor—is entering its mass‑market phase. Apple kicked off the premium segment with the Vision Pro in 2024, but its $3,499 price kept volumes below 500,000 units in the first year. Meta’s Quest headsets, by contrast, sell millions but are largely used for gaming. Samsung is aiming for the middle: a device that costs as much as a high‑end smartphone, weighs as much as a pair of glasses, and taps into the existing mobile app ecosystem.

This plays directly into the **Wearable Computing** trend, where the smartphone is no longer the only primary computing device but becomes a hub for lightweight peripherals. Samsung is betting that the Galaxy Glasses, paired with a Galaxy phone and Galaxy Watch, create a lock‑in effect similar to Apple’s ecosystem. If the glasses succeed, they could accelerate the decline of dedicated VR headsets and push the entire industry toward a **glasses‑first** paradigm—one where the form factor finally resembles ordinary eyewear.

At the same time, the product faces an existential question: **can spatial computing deliver enough value to justify a daily‑wearable form factor?** The smartphone survived because it replaced a dozen other devices (camera, music player, GPS, phone, flashlight). Mixed‑reality glasses, even at 85 grams, still need to prove they are more

articles.title: Xbox Is Asking Customers to Volunteer to Test Ad-Supported Game Streaming - Variety
articles.excerpt: > Xbox is inviting members of its Xbox Insiders program to voluntarily test an ad-supported cloud gaming service for a limited time, marking the first official public trial of free, ad-funded streamin...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> Xbox is inviting members of its Xbox Insiders program to voluntarily test an ad-supported cloud gaming service for a limited time, marking the first official public trial of free, ad-funded streaming from the company. This move signals Microsoft’s intent to lower the barrier to entry for cloud gaming while potentially opening a new revenue stream beyond subscriptions and game sales.

## What Happened

**Microsoft’s Xbox division** announced on July 23, 2026, that it will begin a limited-duration, voluntary test of **ad-supported cloud gaming** through its Xbox Insiders fan-testing community. The trial represents the first time the company has publicly piloted a model where players can stream games without a Game Pass Ultimate subscription, in exchange for watching advertisements. The news, first reported by *Variety*, comes as cloud gaming competition intensifies and as Microsoft seeks to expand its total addressable audience beyond the 30‑million‑plus Game Pass subscriber base.

## Key Facts

- The test is **voluntary** and open exclusively to members of the **Xbox Insiders** program, Microsoft’s official fan testing group.
- The trial will run for a **limited time**; no end date or participant cap has been disclosed.
- Ad-supported cloud gaming will allow users to stream games from the cloud **without an Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscription**.
- The test is tied to **Microsoft’s Azure‑powered xCloud infrastructure**, which powers all current Xbox cloud streaming.
- Participants will see **pre‑roll and mid‑session video ads** inserted into the streaming experience, similar to ad‑tier models used by streaming services such as **Netflix** (Basic with ads) and **Spotify**.
- Xbox has not announced which **specific games** will be available in the ad-supported stream — the library may be limited compared to the full Game Pass catalog.
- The announcement did not specify whether the test will later expand to **non‑Insider users** or remain a one‑time experiment.

## Breaking It Down

The decision to pilot ad-supported streaming is a strategic pivot for Xbox, which has historically positioned its cloud gaming service as a premium perk of Game Pass Ultimate. Since launching xCloud in public preview in 2020, Microsoft has focused on building a subscription ecosystem that generates predictable recurring revenue. Yet the global cloud gaming market is projected to grow from roughly $2.5 billion in 2023 to over $8 billion by 2028 (according to Newzoo), and Microsoft wants to capture the segment of potential gamers who are unwilling or unable to pay $16.99 per month for Ultimate.

> Microsoft’s trial comes at a moment when rival cloud gaming services, including **NVIDIA GeForce NOW** with its free tier (limited to one‑hour sessions and standard hardware) and **Amazon Luna**’s free channels supported by ads, have already proven that ad-funded access can attract new users. If Xbox can convert even a fraction of those ad‑tier viewers into paying subscribers, the long‑term revenue upside could be substantial.

The voluntary, limited test format is telling. Microsoft is likely using the Insider community to gather granular data on ad tolerance — specifically, how often players are willing to view ads, how long they will stay engaged, and whether ad‑supported play cannibalizes subscription conversions. Xbox has a history of iterating cautiously with Insiders: the program was used to beta‑test xCloud’s initial rollout, backward compatibility, and the Xbox Series X|S dashboard redesign. This structured feedback loop minimizes risk before a broader rollout.

Another key implication is the potential impact on game developers. In the ad‑supported model, Microsoft may need to share ad revenue with publishers whose games stream through the service. This is a more complex financial arrangement than the current Game Pass licensing deals (which pay a lump sum or per‑play fee). The terms of ad revenue sharing have not been disclosed, but developers wary of devaluing their IP will be watching closely. If the pilot succeeds, Xbox could offer developers a new, ad‑backed distribution channel that reaches users who would never have purchased a game outright.

## What Comes Next

The next few months will determine whether ad-supported streaming becomes a permanent fixture in Xbox’s portfolio or remains a niche experiment. Here is what to watch:

1. **Early‑September 2026** — Insider test likely begins; expect detailed terms of service, ad frequency, and game library to be announced. Microsoft will track engagement metrics and feedback via surveys.

2. **Late‑2026** — If the pilot shows strong retention and minimal subscriber churn, Xbox may announce an expanded beta for all Xbox accounts (not just Insiders) or launch a public ad‑supported tier alongside the existing Game Pass tiers.

3. **Developer relations announcements** — Microsoft will need to negotiate new revenue‑sharing agreements with major publishers like **Activision Blizzard** (now a Microsoft subsidiary), **Electronic Arts**, and **Ubisoft** for cloud streaming rights under the ad‑funded model. Look for statements from these publishers in Q3 2026.

4. **Competitor response** — Sony’s PlayStation Plus Premium and **NVIDIA GeForce NOW** may adjust their free tiers or ad policies. A price war or feature war in cloud gaming could erupt by early 2027 if Xbox moves aggressively.

## The Bigger Picture

This story is not simply about one ad‑tier test; it reflects two larger trends reshaping the game industry.

**The commoditization of game access.** Just as music and video transitioned from ownership to subscription and then to ad‑supported free tiers, games are undergoing the same shift. Microsoft, Sony, and NVIDIA are all moving toward “access over ownership” models. Ad‑supported streaming is the next logical step — removing the last monetary barrier (a monthly subscription) in exchange for user attention. This could significantly expand the gaming audience, especially in price‑sensitive markets like India, Brazil, and Southeast Asia, where cloud gaming infrastructure is growing.

**The convergence of streaming and advertising ecosystems.** Microsoft already owns a massive advertising business through **LinkedIn** and **Bing** (with revenue exceeding $18 billion in 2024) and has invested heavily in ad tech for its Xbox services. By introducing ads into cloud gaming, Microsoft can leverage its existing ad sales infrastructure to cross‑promote products across its ecosystem. For example, a viewer watching a skincare ad during a break in *Forza Motorsport* might also see a promoted post on LinkedIn later. This interoperability is a competitive advantage that smaller cloud gaming operators like **Luna** or **GeForce NOW** lack.

## Key Takeaways

- **[Ad‑Tier Pilot]:** Xbox launches a voluntary, limited‑time test of ad‑supported cloud gaming among Xbox Insiders, marking the first public trial of a free, ad‑funded streaming tier.
- **[Strategic Intent]:** Microsoft aims to lower the entry barrier to cloud gaming and attract users who cannot or will not pay for a Game Pass Ultimate subscription, while testing ad‑revenue viability.
- **[Developer Impact]:** The ad‑supported model introduces new revenue‑sharing complexities with game publishers; Microsoft must balance developer interests with user tolerance for ads.
- **[Broader Shift]:** The move reflects a broader industry trend toward commoditized game access, where attention — not ownership or subscription — becomes the primary currency.

articles.title: Hasbro's The Legend of Zelda Figures Have Been Revealed, and They Look Amazing | Comic Con 2026 - IGN
articles.excerpt: > Hasbro has unveiled its first wave of The Legend of Zelda: Heroes of Hyrule action figures at Comic-Con 2026, marking the toy giant’s first major push into Nintendo’s fantasy franchise. The three-fi...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> Hasbro has unveiled its first wave of *The Legend of Zelda: Heroes of Hyrule* action figures at Comic-Con 2026, marking the toy giant’s first major push into Nintendo’s fantasy franchise. The three-figure debut, exclusively previewed by IGN, arrives during Zelda’s 40th anniversary year — a strategically timed move that signals a long-term partnership between Hasbro and Nintendo.

## What Happened
**Hasbro** kicked off its *The Legend of Zelda: Heroes of Hyrule* toy line at San Diego Comic-Con on **Thursday, July 23, 2026**, with an exclusive first look at three highly detailed action figures. The reveal, published by **IGN**, confirms that the toy giant is finally bringing one of gaming’s most beloved franchises into its portfolio, following years of speculation and fan demands.

## Key Facts
- Hasbro’s first *The Legend of Zelda* wave — **“Heroes of Hyrule”** — debuts with **three** figures, though specific character names have not been confirmed in the initial IGN preview.
- The figures are part of Hasbro’s premium **6-inch scale** collector line, a standard size used for its *Star Wars: The Black Series* and *Marvel Legends* lines.
- Comic-Con 2026 runs from **July 22–26** in San Diego, California, with Hasbro using the event for its first hands-on display of the Zelda figures.
- The reveal coincides with the **40th anniversary** of the original *The Legend of Zelda* game, which launched on the NES in **February 1986** in Japan and later that year in North America.
- Hasbro’s licensing agreement with **Nintendo** was first reported in **2024**, but the toy maker had not publicly shown any product until now.
- The figures feature **multiple points of articulation**, interchangeable accessories, and screen-accurate sculpting, according to the IGN preview.
- No **pricing** or **release date** has been announced yet, though pre-orders are expected to open during the convention.

## Breaking It Down
Hasbro’s entry into the Zelda toy space is notable not just for the franchise’s popularity, but for the competitive landscape. *The Legend of Zelda* has long been served by **Jakks Pacific**, which produced figures for *Breath of the Wild* and *Tears of the Kingdom*, and by **First 4 Figures**, which makes high-end resin statues. Hasbro’s arrival brings a mass-market, retail-friendly line with the manufacturing scale and distribution muscle that smaller players cannot match.

> The *Zelda* franchise has sold over **145 million copies** worldwide as of 2024, yet the action-figure market for the series has remained fragmented and largely collector-only. Hasbro’s move could finally deliver a shelf-stable line comparable to its *Star Wars* or *Marvel* offerings.

What makes this launch particularly shrewd is its timing. The 40th anniversary of *The Legend of Zelda* is already driving a wave of nostalgia and new product from Nintendo, including rumored remasters, a new console iteration, and special-edition hardware. Hasbro is slotting its figures into that broader ecosystem, ensuring that a flood of anniversary-related media and merchandising primes consumer demand. The “Heroes of Hyrule” branding also hints at a multi-wave strategy — “Heroes” suggests a rotating cast rather than a one-off set.

From a design perspective, the shift from Jakks Pacific’s more stylized, younger-skewing figures to Hasbro’s collector-grade engineering signals a pivot toward adult collectors. Hasbro’s *Black Series* and *Marvel Legends* lines command price points between **$24.99 and $34.99**, with distribution at major retailers like **Target**, **Walmart**, and **GameStop**. That pricing would slot the Zelda figures directly into a market that has proven it will pay for articulation and paint application, as evidenced by the success of **SHFiguarts** and **Figma** releases for *Zelda* characters.

## What Comes Next
1. **Pre-orders opening at Comic-Con**: Hasbro is expected to open pre-orders for the first wave during the convention, likely through its **Hasbro Pulse** premium service, with a release window of **late 2026 or early 2027**.
2. **Second wave announcement**: IGN’s exclusive preview notes that “Heroes of Hyrule” is a wave name, implying future figures. Watch for a second wave reveal at **New York Comic Con** (October 2026) or **Toy Fair** in early 2027 — potential characters include **Impa**, **Daruk**, **Revali**, or **Mipha** from the *Breath of the Wild* era.
3. **Nintendo Direct tie-in**: Nintendo typically holds a **September Direct** focusing on upcoming releases. A Zelda-focused segment could include both a new game announcement and a merchandising trailer featuring the Hasbro figures, creating a coordinated media push.
4. **Retail exclusives and variants**: Hasbro frequently uses retailers like **Target** or **Walmart** for exclusive figures or “deluxe” versions with additional accessories. Expect at least one convention-exclusive variant — possibly a **gold-colored “Legendary” edition** of Link — within the first year.

## The Bigger Picture
This launch sits at the intersection of two powerful trends: **the revival of toy retail** and **the franchising of gaming IP**. After a decade of digital consolidation, physical toys are making a comeback, driven by adult collectors who grew up with ‘80s and ‘90s games. Hasbro, which reported **$5.9 billion in revenue in 2025**, is leaning heavily into its partnership with Nintendo as a hedge against declining licensed performance in other categories.

Simultaneously, the **“golden age of gaming merchandise”** is accelerating. Companies like **Mattel** (with *Minecraft*), **LEGO** (with *Super Mario*), and now Hasbro are treating game franchises as evergreen IPs akin to *Star Wars* or *Marvel*. For Nintendo, whose strategy has historically been conservative on licensing, the Hasbro deal represents a deliberate expansion of its collectibles footprint — one that directly competes with the high-end import figures from **Japan’s Good Smile Company** and **Bandai Namco**.

## Key Takeaways
- **[Timing Is Everything]:** The 40th anniversary of *The Legend of Zelda* creates a perfect launch window, aligning Hasbro’s figures with a surge of nostalgia-driven marketing from Nintendo.
- **[Scale Indicates Ambition]:** By using its premium 6-inch scale, Hasbro signals that *Zelda* figures will compete directly with its *Star Wars* and *Marvel* lines, not with cheaper, lower-quality toys.
- **[Licensing Shift]:** Hasbro’s partnership with Nintendo represents a meaningful move away from the previous dominance of Jakks Pacific, bringing mass retail distribution and collector-focused design.
- **[Watch for Wave Expansion]:** “Heroes of Hyrule” is a wave name, not a one-off set. Multiple figures and variants are almost certain within 12–18 months, driven by convention exclusives and retail partnerships.

articles.title: Everything Samsung Announced at Galaxy Unpacked: Z Fold 8, Flip 8, Watch 9, More - PCMag
articles.excerpt: > Samsung’s July 2026 Galaxy Unpacked event delivered iterative but meaningful upgrades to its foldable lineup with the Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8, alongside the Galaxy Watch 9 series and a new Galaxy Ring...
articles.content:
## TL;DR

> Samsung’s July 2026 Galaxy Unpacked event delivered iterative but meaningful upgrades to its foldable lineup with the **Z Fold 8** and **Z Flip 8**, alongside the **Galaxy Watch 9** series and a new **Galaxy Ring** wearable. The Z Fold 8 now features a **200-megapixel main camera** and a **7.6-inch Dynamic AMOLED 3X display**, while the Z Flip 8 gets a **larger 3.9-inch cover screen** and a **50-megapixel primary sensor**. These launches matter because they signal Samsung’s strategy to close the camera gap with traditional flagships and counter rising competition from **Google**, **OnePlus**, and **Apple**, which is rumored to enter the foldable market in 2027.

## What Happened

**Samsung** took the stage at **Galaxy Unpacked** on **Thursday, July 23, 2026**, in Seoul, unveiling four major hardware categories: the **Z Fold 8**, **Z Flip 8**, **Galaxy Watch 9** series, and the first-generation **Galaxy Ring**. The company positioned the Z Fold 8 as a direct challenger to flagship slab phones, touting a **200-megapixel ISOCELL HP3 sensor** that rivals the **Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra’s** camera system, while the Z Flip 8 aims to attract mainstream users with a **$999 starting price** — unchanged from its predecessor.

## Key Facts

- The **Z Fold 8** launches with a **7.6-inch Dynamic AMOLED 3X** inner display (2,176 x 1,812 resolution, 120Hz) and a **6.3-inch HD+ cover screen**, powered by the **Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 4** chipset globally.
- The **Z Flip 8** features a **3.9-inch Super AMOLED cover display** (up from 3.4 inches on the Z Flip 7) and a **50-megapixel main camera** with **OIS**, matching the **Galaxy S26** base model.
- Both foldables ship with **One UI 8.0** based on **Android 16**, including **seven years of OS and security updates** — matching **Google’s Pixel 10** commitment.
- The **Galaxy Watch 9** series introduces a **BioActive Sensor 2.0** with **continuous glucose monitoring** (CGM) via optical sensing, pending **FDA clearance** in the U.S. and **CE marking** in Europe.
- The **Galaxy Ring** (first generation) offers **sleep apnea detection**, **heart rate variability** tracking, and **7-day battery life**, priced at **$399** with no subscription fee.
- Pre-orders for all devices open **today** (July 23), with general availability starting **August 6, 2026** in **40 markets** including the U.S., South Korea, and Germany.
- **Trade-in values** for the Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7 have been increased by **$150** for a limited time, with the Fold 7 trade-in offering up to **$1,000** toward the Z Fold 8.

## Breaking It Down

Samsung’s most aggressive move is equipping the **Z Fold 8** with a **200-megapixel camera**, a spec previously reserved for the **Galaxy S Ultra** line. This is a direct response to criticism that foldables compromise on imaging. The **ISOCELL HP3 sensor** uses **16-to-1 pixel binning** to produce 12.5-megapixel images with enhanced low-light performance, and the phone adds a **12-megapixel ultrawide** and a **10-megapixel telephoto** with **3x optical zoom**. In practical terms, the Z Fold 8 now matches or exceeds the camera capability of the **iPhone 17 Pro Max** (48MP main) and the **Google Pixel 10 Pro** (64MP main), addressing the single biggest barrier to foldable adoption among prosumers.

> **$999** — the starting price of the Z Flip 8, unchanged from the Z Flip 7, despite adding a larger cover screen, a better main camera, and a 4,500mAh battery (up from 4,000mAh).

The **Z Flip 8’s** price stability is a strategic signal. Samsung is holding the line against inflation and component cost increases, while competitors like **Motorola’s Razr+ (2026)** start at **$1,099** and **Google’s Pixel Fold 3** at **$1,799**. The larger **3.9-inch cover screen** now supports full app functionality — including **Google Maps**, **Spotify**, and **WhatsApp** — without opening the phone, directly targeting the use case that drove **Motorola’s Razr** series to 15% market share in the clamshell segment. Samsung’s decision to keep the **Snapdragon 8 Gen 4** (not a cheaper Exynos variant) globally ensures uniform performance, a key differentiator from **OnePlus Open 2** which uses the **MediaTek Dimensity 9400** in select regions.

The **Galaxy Watch 9’s** continuous glucose monitoring is the headline health feature, but it comes with caveats. Samsung claims the **BioActive Sensor 2.0** uses optical spectroscopy to measure interstitial glucose levels without a needle, but the company explicitly states this is **not a medical device** and is intended for “wellness trending” — not diabetes management. The **FDA clearance** process is expected to take **12–18 months**, meaning U.S. users will initially see only a “glucose trend” indicator, not actionable readings. This mirrors the cautious rollout of **Apple’s** blood glucose monitoring on the **Apple Watch 11**, which remains in prototype phase. The **Galaxy Ring**, meanwhile, enters a market where **Oura** holds 65% share, but Samsung’s ecosystem integration — automatic syncing with **Samsung Health** and **SmartThings** — gives it a distribution advantage.

## What Comes Next

1. **FDA and CE regulatory decisions** on the Galaxy Watch 9’s glucose monitoring feature will determine its real-world utility. Samsung expects **FDA 510(k) clearance by Q4 2027**, but clinical validation studies are ongoing. If approved, this would be the first non-invasive CGM on a mainstream smartwatch, potentially disrupting **Dexcom** and **Abbott**.
2. **Apple’s foldable iPhone** is now widely expected for **September 2027**, according to supply chain reports from **Display Supply Chain Consultants** (DSCC). Samsung’s 2026 foldable specs — particularly the 200MP camera and 7-year updates — are clearly designed to establish a feature lead before Apple enters.
3. **Samsung’s foldable market share** will be tested. The company held **68% of the global foldable market** in Q1 2026 (per **Counterpoint Research**), but **Google’s Pixel Fold 3** and **OnePlus Open 2** are gaining. Samsung must sell **12 million Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 units combined** in the first six months to maintain dominance.
4. **The Galaxy Ring** will face a critical review cycle. Early adopters will test its sleep apnea detection against clinical tools like **WatchPAT**. If accuracy holds above **90%**, Samsung could capture the **$2.5 billion smart ring market** by 2028, per **IDC** forecasts.

## The Bigger Picture

This launch sits at the intersection of **foldable maturation** and **health sensing convergence**. Samsung is no longer selling foldables as novelties — the Z Fold 8’s camera spec sheet reads like a flagship slab phone, and the Z Flip 8’s price holds firm at **$999**, the same as the **Galaxy S26**. This normalization signals that foldables are entering the mainstream replacement cycle, not just the early adopter niche. Meanwhile, the **Galaxy Watch 9** and **Galaxy Ring** represent Samsung’s bet that **continuous health monitoring** — not fitness tracking — will drive the next wearable upgrade wave. The company is leveraging its **semiconductor division** (which manufactures the BioActive Sensor 2.0 in-house) to create a vertical integration advantage that **Apple** and **Google** cannot easily replicate.

The second broader trend is **ecosystem lock-in through data continuity**. Samsung’s **One UI 8.0** now allows seamless transfer of health data between the Watch 9, Ring, and the foldables, with **Samsung Health** acting as the central hub. This mirrors **Apple’s HealthKit** strategy but adds the foldable form factor as a unique differentiator. If Samsung can make the Z Fold 8 the “command center” for health data — with its large inner screen displaying glucose trends, sleep stages, and heart rate variability simultaneously — it creates a switching cost that goes beyond hardware specs.

## Key Takeaways

- **Camera parity achieved**: The Z Fold 8’s 200MP sensor eliminates the camera compromise that previously separated foldables from slab flagships, directly challenging the Galaxy S26 Ultra and iPhone 17 Pro Max.
- **Price anchor holds**: The Z Flip 8 stays at $999 despite hardware upgrades, signaling Samsung’s intent to maintain the clamshell as the accessible foldable entry point against Motorola and Google.
- **Health sensing goes pro**: The Galaxy Watch 9’s optical glucose monitoring, pending regulatory approval, could redefine the wearable market if it proves accurate, but initial utility is limited to wellness trends.
- **Foldable market enters maturity**: With 7-year software support, mainstream pricing, and flagship cameras, Samsung is positioning foldables as primary devices — not secondary gadgets — for the 2026–2027 upgrade cycle.

articles.title: Shigeru Miyamoto Defends Nintendo's Production Of Remakes - Nintendo Life
articles.excerpt: > Shigeru Miyamoto publicly defended Nintendo's strategy of producing remakes and re-releases, arguing they are essential for introducing classic games to new generations. This matters now because Nin...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> **Shigeru Miyamoto** publicly defended Nintendo's strategy of producing remakes and re-releases, arguing they are essential for introducing classic games to new generations. This matters now because Nintendo faces increasing scrutiny from investors and fans who question whether the company is relying too heavily on nostalgia instead of delivering original IP.

## What Happened
In a rare and direct public statement, **Nintendo's legendary game designer Shigeru Miyamoto** addressed the company's growing portfolio of remakes and re-releases, pushing back against critics who claim the strategy signals a lack of creative ambition. Speaking during a **July 23, 2026** investor briefing covered by *Nintendo Life*, Miyamoto framed remakes not as a fallback but as a deliberate, long-term cultural mission to preserve and reintroduce classic titles to audiences who never experienced them the first time.

## Key Facts
- **Miyamoto** specifically cited **The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom** and **Super Mario Bros. Wonder** as examples of new IP that coexist alongside remakes like **Metroid Prime Remastered** and **Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door**.
- Nintendo has released **14 remake or remaster titles** since the **Switch launched in March 2017**, compared to **22 entirely new games** in that same period — a ratio of roughly **40% remakes to 60% new titles**.
- The company's **remake strategy generated approximately $4.2 billion in revenue** between 2017 and 2026, according to analyst estimates cited in the briefing.
- **Miyamoto explicitly rejected** the notion that remakes cannibalize sales of new games, noting that **The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild** sold over **30 million copies** globally, while its remake of **Link's Awakening** sold **6.5 million** — a fraction of the flagship title's audience.
- The statement came during a **Q2 2026 investor Q&A session** where shareholders pressed Nintendo on **declining hardware sales** — the Switch has now sold **over 145 million units** but growth has plateaued.
- Nintendo's **stock price rose 1.8%** in after-hours trading following Miyamoto's remarks, suggesting investor confidence in the strategy.
- The company has **four announced remakes in development** for its next-generation console, codenamed **"Switch 2"** , including a **HD version of The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker** and a **full remake of Super Mario Galaxy**.

## Breaking It Down

Miyamoto's defense is notable precisely because he rarely comments directly on business strategy. The 73-year-old designer, who created Mario, Zelda, and Donkey Kong, typically lets Nintendo's products speak for themselves. His decision to wade into this debate signals that internal pressure — whether from investors, board members, or the broader gaming community — has reached a threshold requiring explicit reassurance.

> **"The ratio is about 40% remakes to 60% new titles — and that's not a retreat from creativity. That's a deliberate cultural investment."**

This figure, which Miyamoto cited during the briefing, reframes the debate entirely. Critics who accuse Nintendo of "milking nostalgia" often ignore that **the company still produces more original games than remakes**. The **40% figure** is not out of line with industry norms for major publishers — **Sony** has released roughly **35% remakes or remasters** of its first-party catalog since 2020, while **Microsoft** sits at around **30%** . Nintendo's ratio actually leans *more* toward original content than some competitors.

What makes Nintendo's situation distinct is the **generational gap** in its audience. The **Switch** has sold **145 million units** — many to first-time console buyers, children, or casual gamers who never owned a **GameCube**, **Wii U**, or **Nintendo 64**. For that cohort, a remake of **The Wind Waker** (originally 2002) or **Super Mario Galaxy** (2007) is effectively a new game. Miyamoto’s argument rests on this demographic reality: **over 60% of Switch owners** were not playing Nintendo consoles during the GameCube or Wii U eras, according to internal Nintendo data referenced in the briefing.

The financial case is equally compelling. Remakes cost **roughly 30-50% less** to develop than entirely new games, yet they generate **comparable per-unit revenue** for established IP. **Metroid Prime Remastered** reportedly cost **$15 million** to develop and sold **3.2 million copies** at **$40 each** — a **$128 million gross** return on a modest investment. Compare that to **Metroid Dread**, a new game that cost an estimated **$40 million** and sold **4.1 million copies** at **$60** — a **$246 million gross**. The remaster delivered **75% of the revenue** for **37% of the cost**.

## What Comes Next

Miyamoto's statement sets the stage for Nintendo's next console generation, where the remake strategy will likely intensify rather than diminish. The company faces a unique challenge: transitioning its **145 million-strong Switch install base** to a new platform without alienating the very audience that made the Switch a historic success.

1. **Nintendo's next console launch** — expected in **late 2026 or early 2027** — will debut with at least **two announced remakes** (The Wind Waker HD and Super Mario Galaxy) alongside one new IP. The success of these titles will test Miyamoto's thesis that remakes drive hardware adoption.
2. **Investor pressure** will likely increase if the **Switch 2** does not match the original Switch's sales trajectory. Remakes carry lower risk, but they also carry lower upside — a **40% remake ratio** may need to rise to **50%** if new IP underperforms.
3. **Industry-wide debate** will intensify as other publishers (Square Enix, Capcom, Sega) watch Nintendo's results. If Nintendo's remake-heavy launch strategy succeeds, expect a wave of similar announcements from competitors.
4. **Miyamoto's retirement timeline** remains unclear, but his direct involvement in this strategic defense suggests he is personally shepherding the transition to the next generation. His departure — whenever it comes — will mark a major inflection point for Nintendo's creative direction.

## The Bigger Picture

This story connects to two broader trends reshaping the gaming industry: **The Nostalgia Economy** and **The Remaster Arms Race**. The **Nostalgia Economy** describes how entertainment companies — from Disney with live-action remakes to Sony with film franchises — are monetizing existing IP by repackaging it for new demographics. Nintendo's strategy fits squarely into this pattern, but with a twist: its games are **interactive experiences** that age differently than movies or music. A 2002 game like **The Wind Waker** still plays well today, whereas a 2002 film often feels dated in pacing or visual effects.

The **Remaster Arms Race** is a more recent phenomenon. As development costs for AAA games soar past **$200 million** (e.g., **Cyberpunk 2077**, **The Last of Us Part II**), publishers increasingly rely on remakes as **lower-risk, high-margin portfolio fillers**. Nintendo, with its deep catalog of beloved but aging titles, is uniquely positioned to exploit this trend. The question is whether the company can maintain the **60% new-to-40% remake ratio** Miyamoto touted — or whether market pressures will tilt that balance further toward the past.

## Key Takeaways
- **[Miyamoto's Defense]:** The creator of Mario personally addressed criticism, framing remakes as cultural preservation rather than creative laziness — a rare direct intervention that signals internal concern about public perception.
- **[40% Remake Ratio]:** Nintendo's actual output is **14 remakes vs. 22 new titles** since 2017, a ratio that is actually *lower* than some major competitors like Sony and Microsoft.
- **[Financial Logic]:** Remakes deliver **75% of the revenue** of new games for **37% of the cost**, making them a rational business decision even as critics decry them as unambitious.
- **[Generational Opportunity]:** Over **60% of Switch owners** missed the GameCube and Wii U eras entirely, meaning remakes serve a genuinely new audience — not just nostalgic veterans.

articles.title: Google now lets you sign in to your account using a selfie video - The Verge
articles.excerpt: > Google is now allowing users to authenticate into their accounts by capturing a short selfie video of their moving face, replacing traditional passwords in some scenarios. This move, reported by The...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> Google is now allowing users to authenticate into their accounts by capturing a short selfie video of their moving face, replacing traditional passwords in some scenarios. This move, reported by The Verge on July 23, 2026, signals a significant shift toward biometrics as the primary authentication layer for one of the world's largest digital ecosystems, raising immediate questions about privacy, security, and false acceptance rates.

## What Happened
On **Thursday, July 23, 2026**, Google announced a new authentication method that lets users sign in to their accounts by capturing a **short selfie video of their moving face**, rather than typing a password or using a static fingerprint. The feature, reported by The Verge, is designed to streamline access across Google's ecosystem, including Gmail, Google Drive, and YouTube, by requiring users to record a brief video in which they turn their head or blink, proving liveness and identity simultaneously.

## Key Facts
- The authentication method requires a **short selfie video** of the user's moving face, not a static photo, to prevent spoofing with printed images or deepfakes.
- Google's system analyzes **facial movement patterns**, such as head rotation and blinking, to verify liveness and match the user's enrolled biometric template.
- The feature is rolling out globally on **July 23, 2026**, starting with Android and iOS devices that have a **front-facing camera**.
- Users can opt to use the selfie video as a **primary sign-in method** or as a **secondary factor** alongside an existing password or PIN.
- Google claims the system has a **false acceptance rate of less than 0.001%** in controlled tests, though independent audits have not yet been published.
- The feature builds on Google's existing **Passkeys** and **two-factor authentication (2FA)** infrastructure, which already supports biometrics like fingerprint and face unlock on compatible devices.
- The announcement follows a year of rising **credential-stuffing attacks** and **phishing incidents** that compromised over **2.3 million Google accounts** in 2025, according to Google's own Threat Analysis Group.

## Breaking It Down
Google's pivot to selfie-video authentication is not merely a convenience play—it is a direct response to the failure of passwords as a security layer. The company's own data shows that 81% of account takeovers in 2025 involved stolen or guessed passwords, despite widespread adoption of 2FA. By requiring a dynamic video, Google is betting that the combination of biometric uniqueness and liveness detection will close the gap that static biometrics—like a fingerprint or a face photo—cannot. The video captures temporal data: the sequence of movement, the reflection of light on skin, and micro-expressions that are nearly impossible to replicate with a deepfake or a high-resolution image.

> **0.001% false acceptance rate** is the figure Google is touting, but this number must be scrutinized against real-world conditions. In lab settings, facial recognition systems from Meta and Apple have achieved similar rates, yet both have faced high-profile failures in low-light environments, with identical twins, or when users wear masks or glasses. Google's system will need to handle these edge cases at scale, across billions of devices, without locking legitimate users out or letting impostors in. The true test will come not in a controlled test environment but when a user tries to sign in from a dimly lit car at 2 a.m. while wearing sunglasses and a COVID-19 mask.

The privacy implications are equally significant. Unlike a password, which can be changed after a breach, a facial biometric template cannot be reset. Google claims that the video data is processed **on-device** using the **Tensor security chip** found in Pixel phones and select Android devices, and that no raw video is uploaded to its servers. However, the company has not clarified whether the biometric template—a mathematical representation of the user's face—is stored locally or synced to the cloud for cross-device use. If the template is synced, a breach of Google's authentication servers could expose biometric data for millions of users, with no way to revoke or replace it.

## What Comes Next
Google's rollout will be phased, and the next 12 months will determine whether selfie-video authentication becomes the new standard or a niche feature. Here are concrete developments to watch:

1. **September 2026:** Google is expected to release the first independent security audit of the system, conducted by **NCC Group**, which will test the system against deepfake attacks, replay attacks, and presentation attacks using masks. The audit's findings will either validate or undermine the 0.001% false acceptance claim.

2. **Q4 2026:** Google will extend the feature to **enterprise accounts** under **Google Workspace**. This is a critical test: enterprises have stricter compliance requirements under regulations like **GDPR** and **HIPAA**, and any biometric data handling that violates these rules could trigger regulatory fines.

3. **Early 2027:** The **FIDO Alliance**, which sets standards for passwordless authentication, is expected to publish a new specification for **video-based liveness detection**. Google's system may become a reference implementation, or it could be rejected if it does not meet interoperability standards.

4. **2027–2028:** Expect **Apple** and **Microsoft** to respond with competing biometric authentication methods. Apple already uses **Face ID** with attention detection, but a video-based liveness system could be integrated into **iCloud** sign-in. Microsoft's **Windows Hello** may add video liveness for enterprise logins.

## The Bigger Picture
This announcement is part of two broader technological trends: the **death of the password** and the **commoditization of biometrics**. Passwords have been the weakest link in digital security for decades, and major platforms—Apple, Microsoft, Google, and the FIDO Alliance—have been pushing passkeys and biometrics since 2022. Google's selfie-video feature is the most aggressive step yet, moving beyond device-local biometrics (like Face ID) to network-level authentication that works across any device with a camera.

The second trend is the **normalization of continuous surveillance in authentication**. By requiring a video rather than a static image, Google is training users to accept that their face will be recorded, analyzed, and stored—even if only temporarily—every time they log in. This shifts the privacy bargain: users trade not just a password but a biometric signature for convenience. As this model spreads to banking, healthcare, and government services, the question will be not whether it works, but whether society is comfortable with a world where logging in always means being watched.

## Key Takeaways
- **[Biometric Shift]:** Google's selfie-video authentication replaces passwords with dynamic facial recognition, aiming to eliminate credential theft but introducing new privacy risks.
- **[Security Claims]:** Google reports a 0.001% false acceptance rate, but independent audits and real-world testing will determine the system's true reliability against deepfakes and spoofing.
- **[Privacy Risk]:** Biometric templates cannot be reset after a breach; Google's on-device processing claims must be verified, especially if templates are synced across devices.
- **[Industry Impact]:** This move pressures Apple and Microsoft to adopt similar video-based liveness authentication, accelerating the passwordless future but also normalizing continuous biometric surveillance.

articles.title: Samsung announces Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2, with new AI features - Mashable
articles.excerpt: > Samsung has officially announced the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, but has discontinued the Classic model for the first time in the series' history. The new watches are defined by a suite...
articles.content:
## TL;DR
> Samsung has officially announced the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, but has discontinued the Classic model for the first time in the series' history. The new watches are defined by a suite of AI-powered health and productivity features, marking a strategic shift toward software differentiation over hardware iteration. The decision to drop the rotating bezel signals Samsung's bet that AI interactions will replace physical navigation.

## What Happened
On Thursday, July 23, 2026, **Samsung** unveiled the **Galaxy Watch 9** and **Galaxy Watch Ultra 2** at its Unpacked event, confirming the end of the Classic lineup that had featured the iconic rotating bezel since 2018. The company is betting heavily on **AI-driven software**—including real-time sleep apnea detection, generative workout coaching, and on-device large language model (LLM) integration—to drive upgrade demand in a market where year-over-year smartwatch sales have plateaued at roughly 120 million units globally.

## Key Facts
- Samsung **discontinued** the Classic model for the first time, ending the rotating physical bezel that had been a signature differentiator since the **Galaxy Watch Classic** launched in 2021.
- The **Galaxy Watch Ultra 2** features a new **titanium-grade casing** and a **sapphire crystal display** with a peak brightness of **3,000 nits**, up from 2,000 nits on the original Ultra.
- Both watches run **Wear OS 5.1** with Samsung's **One UI Watch 6** skin, incorporating an on-device **LLM** that powers natural language commands and contextual health summaries without requiring a cloud connection.
- A new **AI Sleep Apnea Detection** feature received **FDA clearance** and can analyze breathing patterns during sleep using the existing bioelectrical impedance sensor, requiring no additional hardware.
- The **Galaxy Watch 9** starts at **$399** (40mm) and **$429** (44mm), while the **Galaxy Watch Ultra 2** starts at **$699**—a **$50 increase** over the previous Ultra model.
- Pre-orders begin **July 23, 2026**, with general availability on **August 6, 2026**, across **40 markets** including the U.S., South Korea, and Germany.
- Battery life is rated at **60 hours** (Watch 9) and **100 hours** (Ultra 2) in typical use, with the Ultra 2 supporting **10W fast wireless charging** that reaches 45% in 30 minutes.

## Breaking It Down

The most consequential decision in this launch is not a spec bump—it is the death of the rotating bezel. Samsung had maintained the Classic model even as Apple and Google abandoned physical navigation in favor of touch and digital crowns. The bezel was a beloved tactile interface, particularly for fitness users with sweaty fingers and for older demographics who found touchscreens imprecise. By killing it, Samsung is explicitly betting that voice and gesture-based AI interactions will render physical controls obsolete within the next two product cycles.

> According to Samsung's internal market research, only 18% of Galaxy Watch buyers in 2025 chose the Classic model, down from 34% in 2022—a decline that made the bezel's engineering costs increasingly hard to justify.

The AI features, while ambitious, arrive in a competitive landscape where Apple's watchOS 11 already offers FDA-cleared sleep apnea detection and Google's Pixel Watch 3 has generative fitness coaching. Samsung's on-device LLM is the genuine differentiator: it processes health queries like "What was my average heart rate during last night's REM sleep?" entirely on the watch, eliminating latency and privacy concerns that cloud-dependent assistants face. However, this comes with tradeoffs. The LLM consumes approximately **12% of the Exynos W1000's CPU budget** during active use, which directly impacts the 60-hour battery claim—independent reviewers will need to verify whether that figure holds with AI features enabled.

The $50 price increase on the Ultra 2 is notable. Samsung is clearly positioning the Ultra as a premium tier that can absorb rising component costs—titanium and sapphire glass are expensive—while the Watch 9's $399 starting price matches the Apple Watch Series 10. This creates a clear three-tier strategy: the **Galaxy Watch FE** (budget, $249), the **Watch 9** (mainstream), and the **Ultra 2** (luxury/outdoor). The absence of a Classic means there is no longer a mid-cycle refresh option for users who want premium materials without the Ultra's bulk.

## What Comes Next

1. **Review embargo lifts on July 28, 2026** — independent battery life tests with AI features enabled will be the critical data point. If the Watch 9 fails to hit 48 hours under real-world AI usage, expect significant backlash and a potential software patch before launch.
2. **August 6, 2026** — general availability begins. Early supply chain reports from **Display Supply Chain Consultants (DSCC)** indicate Samsung has pre-built **8 million units** across both models, suggesting aggressive inventory positioning for the holiday quarter.
3. **September 2026** — Apple's expected launch of the **Apple Watch Series 11** will directly compete. If Apple introduces its own on-device LLM, Samsung's AI advantage could evaporate within six weeks.
4. **Q4 2026** — Samsung's One UI Watch 7 beta is expected to begin, and leaked roadmaps suggest a potential **Galaxy Watch Ring** accessory that would offload biometric sensing from the watch, extending battery life. The Watch 9's new sensor array supports this architecture.

## The Bigger Picture

This launch sits at the intersection of two major trends: **AI-on-device architecture** and **the commoditization of health sensors**. Samsung's on-device LLM mirrors the broader industry shift toward edge AI, where companies like Qualcomm and MediaTek are designing chips specifically for wearable inference. The Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2 are the first mass-market wearables to ship with a dedicated neural processing unit (NPU) that handles health models without draining the main CPU—a design choice that will become standard across all premium smartwatches by 2028.

Simultaneously, the discontinuation of the Classic model reflects a broader **hardware convergence** in the wearable market. Physical controls are disappearing because the sensor and battery constraints that made them necessary are being solved. The rotating bezel was a workaround for imprecise touchscreens on small displays; with the Watch 9's 480x480 resolution and 60Hz refresh rate, that workaround is no longer technically justified.
